en: Verses on the Biographies of Virtuous Women, Composed by the Upāsaka under the Bodhisattva Precepts, Peng Jiqing:
I observe all worlds, Which are always characterized by quiescent extinction; How can one dwell amidst these illusory transformations?
Thus the male and female organs arise; it is like the great empty sky. By pressing on the eyes, one sees wild flowers;
these flowers cannot be grasped. They arise from your own deluded thoughts. Deluded thoughts lead into saṃsāra, binding oneself through kalpa after kalpa.
If, in a single thought-moment, you suddenly awaken to yourself, you will realize that delusion has no origin at all.
Even "empty space" is but a forced designation; how could "wild flowers" (floating hairs) ever truly exist?
In the past, the Buddha rebuked women for being replete with all manner of seductive impurities. For those who harbor defiled attachments, their suffering is more severe than that of a prison.
How is it that people in this world, each coveting and loving one another, carry such heavy burdens as to sink into the mire?
Until death one may not escape, like an ant circling in a loop, never leaving the space of a single grindstone.
Now I speak these bitter words, universally exhorting all women:
understand that the cause of rebirth is craving, which is its very root; from craving it is born, and through craving it dies.
At the very moment of craving, every thought-instant is constantly extinguished. If even one's own body does not exist, how much less the body of another?
From this day forth, I resolve upon the Great Mind; I take refuge in the Unsurpassed One who constantly turns the Mahāyāna sūtras.
I shall diligently practice according to what is taught. As for those people of excessive measure—
Explosively shattering the delusions of ignorance, one enters suddenly into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

gradually purifying all remaining habitual tendencies, there is yet another extraordinary expedient: single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha, one entrusts one’s substance to a wondrous lotus flower and swiftly attains non-retrogression.
All the sutras fully expound this, and all the patriarchs together uphold it.
Only she among women was noble, Having attained this fruit of purity.

How could a great man willingly become a walking corpse? I now relate this narrative, To be circulated far and wide, universally exhorting all sentient beings To forever sever the root of saṃsāra. Namo Buddhāya!
Preface to the Biographies of Virtuous Women from the Kingdom of Jiaozhi:

Regarding the transmission of these biographies, laymen are not ranked alongside kings; originally, those of the supreme dignity of the "Nine and Five" (the Emperor) may not be placed in the same class as common subjects.
Regarding those who extensively protected the Triple Gem and deeply accorded with the One Vehicle, their deeds are fully recorded in the dynastic histories and the *Fozu Tongji*;

as these accounts are clear, there is no need for further elaboration. As for the consorts and empresses of successive reigns, although their status was close to that of the Sovereign, [their contributions were likewise significant].
Nevertheless, there is no established tradition for concluding their accounts; in principle, they are treated on par with the conduct of ministers.
Furthermore, as their deeds mostly lie between the manifest and the obscure, I have therefore set them forth in this book to serve as an exhortation for those who occupy high positions.
The *Fozu tongji* records that Empress Gudu of the Sui dynasty was devoted to the cultivation of pure karma (*śukla-karma*).

At the time of her death, an extraordinary fragrance filled the chamber and a radiance like clouds appeared as she departed toward the west. I have examined the *Sui shu*, which states that the empress was jealous by nature and secretly killed palace women who gained favor with the Emperor.
Now, a compassionate heart that refrains from killing is the foremost of pure karmas; yet, if the karma of killing is not eliminated, how can one attain such a death?
An hopes for rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, the source of this account is not detailed; it is feared to be an error in transmission, so it has been excised.

Ye Xiaolan’s life story borders on the miraculous, yet its underlying principle is most ordinary and free from doubt. Moreover, she abandoned the path of the immortals to pursue the Buddha, her power of wisdom being preeminent.
Her examination of the precepts and her responses were sincere acts of repentance; they might otherwise have been compared merely to those of the Six Dynasties.
To explain it in this way is to lose its essential meaning. As for his own liberation and that of others, he took the severing of attachment as the fundamental principle;
in capturing the enemy, he seized the king. He possessed the strategic prowess of a true man. Those with the aspiration to transcend the world must urgently fix their eyes upon this point.
The accounts of miraculous responses recorded in various texts have been cited repeatedly, with each subsequent version adding more details until they gradually lost their original integrity.
Now, I have relied solely on the original sources; I have merely excised redundant passages and replaced colloquial expressions, ensuring that nothing essential to the core meaning is compromised.

As for those instances where the literary embellishment exceeds the substance, where the false confuses the true, and which follow the style of trivial official records or minor fiction—these have not been included.
What I have not dared to include is found in the various works cited herein, such as the *Mingxiang ji*, the *Baoying ji*, and the *Jingtu jiyao*. Complete versions of these have not been seen;
they appear fragmentarily in the *Taiping guangji* and the *Langgan ji*. Now, I have identified and noted the titles of their original sources.
This is what consciousness originates from. Other cases may be inferred by analogy.
The words and phrases of the Zen school all flow forth from within self-nature; they cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination.
Readers who harbor doubts regarding this should deeply investigate and diligently research it; there will naturally be a point of entry.

One must not hastily harbor thoughts of withdrawal or rest, nor should one forcibly fabricate realizations or interpretations, which would lead to misrepresenting the Prajñāpāramitā and severing one's roots of goodness forever. The implications are no small matter;
be careful, be careful!

In the first volume of the *Shannüzhuan* (Biographies of Virtuous Women), Zhinui says: From the Han dynasty onwards, those who compiled biographies of virtuous women generally prioritized the traditional compliance of a wife.
It was only in later times that exceptionally outstanding and extraordinary conduct emerged; when one examines their resolve and integrity, it is as bright and clear as ice and frost.
Is it not as if one were about to ride the *gāng* winds, control the *hào* breath, and soar through the Pure Capital (*Qīngdū*)?

For those who truly wish to sever the flow of birth and death and ascend to the shore of *nirvāṇa*, they must necessarily settle their spirits in the field of tranquil stillness and take lofty flight beyond the realms of humans and devas.
Unless one has long planted pure causes and possesses firm vows, there is none who will not falter and draw back in self-defeat.
Furthermore, having already compiled the *Biographies of Lay Practitioners* (*Jushi zhuan*), I subsequently bestowed various Mahāyāna sūtras upon two young women. Consequently,
I continued to collect accounts of approximately one hundred and thirty virtuous women from both ancient and modern times who entered the stream of the Dharma,
compiling them into a single biography which I gave to the two women, so that they might transmit and study it.
Yang Tiāohuá was the daughter of Yang Déshèn of Dōngguǎn during the Jin dynasty. From her youth, she possessed both talent and beauty.

She had been betrothed to Wáng Xī, a man from the same commandery, but before the marriage could be consummated, both Tiāohuá’s parents passed away in succession, and Wáng Xī also lost his mother. Suddenly, she realized the impermanence of life.
He immediately renounced secular life to become a monk, changing his name to Sengdu.
Once Tiāohuā had completed her mourning period, she wrote a letter to Du, stating that one’s hair and skin must not be mutilated and the ancestral sacrifices must not be abruptly discontinued.

She urged him to heed worldly teachings and revise his far-reaching aspirations, so as to assist this era of great brilliance, honor the spirits of his ancestors, and satisfy the wishes of both gods and men. She also presented him with five poems, the first of which says: [Poem omitted]
A human life spent within this world is as fleeting as the wind passing through a window. Upon the riverbank, there is the lingering chant;

as the sun slants, one thinks of beating the barrel drum. Its pure tones can delight the ear; its flavors can satisfy the palate; fine silks can adorn the body; and a splendid crown can illuminate the head.
"Your Reverence has taken up the tonsure for yourself, devoting yourself to emptiness to the detriment of existence. You do not consider my humble situation;

I only pray that you will show compassion for me hereafter. In his reply, Sengduo said: "Now, serving a ruler to bring order to a single state does not compare to extending one’s great vow to save the myriad realms.
Serving one’s parents to establish a single household does not compare to propagating the Great Way to save the three worlds. However, my virtue does not reach far, and I have not yet—"

I am able to share this with you, yet I feel some shame in doing so. Nevertheless, just as a mountain is formed by the accumulation of baskets of earth, I also hope that what is minute may eventually become manifest.

Furthermore, when one wears the *kāṣāya*, shakes the *khakkhara* staff, drinks from clear streams, and tastes the flavor of *prajñā*, even the robes of kings and dukes, the feasts of the eight delicacies, the clanging sounds of music, and the brilliant splendor of ornaments cannot compare to it. If we can reach a profound accord, then let us aim for the same goal together.

He entered nirvana. Furthermore, he composed five stanzas of poetry to express his own resolve. Tiāohuá was moved to realization and likewise maintained the Way until the end of her life (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Lady Ji was the wife of Ge Jizhi of Ju’rong. She lived during the Liu Song dynasty.

While the Ge family had followed the lineage of Ge Xuanzhi (Zhichuan) for generations in studying the arts of immortality, Lady Ji alone took delight in the Buddha-dharma; she maintained her sincerity without fail.

One day, while she was weaving, she looked up and saw the clouds parting to reveal a bright sun, and the air became clear and serene. Suddenly, precious canopies, banners, and streamers came from the west, appearing in the midst of the sky.
There was an *Tathāgata* embracing her, his golden body radiating so brightly that it illuminated the space beyond the clouds. Ji stood still at her loom and gazed intently;
her heart leaped with joy as she exclaimed, "The sutras speak of the Buddha of Infinite Life—could this be him? She then prostrated herself in worship.
Ji then led her to point out the location of the Buddha, but she saw only half the body and various banners and canopies, which suddenly vanished.
At that time, the elders and children of the village all witnessed and heard this, and those who followed her to take refuge in the Buddha were very numerous (*Mingxiang ji*).
A woman of the Wei clan from Liangjun had both father and elder brother practicing the pure karma; the woman herself was also resolute in her aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Before long, she passed away, but after seven days she revived. She immediately ascended a high seat and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Having finished, she descended and addressed [the assembly]:
The father said, "Child, go. He then went to the pool of seven treasures in the Land of Immeasurable Life.

The child, along with his father and elder brother, each had a great lotus flower within which they were to be born; however, his mother alone was without one. Unable to bear this grief, she has come to inform you.
Having finished speaking, she closed her eyes and passed away. From that time on, her mother also came to revere the Dharma (*Mingxiang ji*).
Fei, the wife of Luo Yu, was a native of Ningzhou and Shuzhou; she was the daughter of Yue, the Regional Inspector of Ningzhou during the Song dynasty.

Fei had revered the Buddha-dharma since her youth and had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for several years. She once suffered from a mental illness and was on the verge of death. She said to those close to her: "I..."

He recited the sutras with such earnest devotion that he was surely to receive auspicious protection; thus, he did not die suddenly. Having fainted, he revived again and said that he had seen the Buddha through the window, extending his hand to stroke his chest.
Instantly, his illness vanished. A man and woman in the same hall all beheld a golden light illuminating the room, and a wondrous fragrance wafted sweetly.
When Yu’s younger sister came to visit him during his illness, she witnessed this spiritual response and gave rise to deep faith.
She observed the fasts and precepts for her entire life, and she constantly used this matter to convert and guide her children and grandchildren (*Shuyiji*).
Ding Guipin of the Liang dynasty, whose given name was Lingguang, was a native of Qiao. She was born in Fancheng; a divine light filled her room at birth, so she was named Guang.
A physiognomist said, "This girl shall attain great nobility. During the Yongtai era of the Qi dynasty, Emperor Wu of the Liang visited Xiangyang.

Yang heard of this and took her in; she was fourteen years old at the time. Empress Xi was by nature suspicious and harsh, yet the Noble Consort was cautious, reverent, and humble, never once incurring reprimand or punishment.
She gave birth to a son, Tong, who became the Crown Prince Zhaoming.

When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, he appointed the Noble Consort to a rank above the Three Ladies, and she resided in the Xianyang Palace. The Noble Consort’s surname was Renshu; she treated all those in attendance with kindness and forbearance.
She won the hearts of all. She did not delight in elaborate adornments, and her vessels and clothing lacked anything precious or beautiful.

When Emperor Wu promoted Buddhism, the Noble Consort (Guīpín) reverently followed his lead. She strictly abstained from pungent roots and meat. On the day she received the precepts, sweet dew descended before the palace hall.

Regarding the scriptural principles established by Emperor Wu, she grasped their essential intent; she was particularly proficient in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra. As for the offerings and gifts she received—

She dedicated everything to support the Dharma activities. She passed away in the seventh year of the Putong era [526 CE]. Her posthumous title was Mu (according to the *Liang Shu*). Lady Wang was a person of the Sui dynasty;
she was the wife of Elder Xue and the mother of the nun Denggai. She recited various sutras and diligently practiced the methods of repentance, aspiring to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty [637 CE], she fell ill. Her earnest devotion reached its peak, and suddenly she saw a bed—
First, a red lotus appeared, as large as a five-oku jar. Then, blue lotuses were seen filling the entire room.
Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta descended into the air. His grandson, Daxing, was standing by his side;
he saw that the Buddha’s body was so tall and vast that it towered above the two Bodhisattvas. After a long while, they vanished, and the Wang family passed away (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Lady Doulu, née Sīn, was the elder sister of the Tang Duke of Rui, Doulu Kuān. She was married to the Duke of Chén. She had long cultivated meritorious deeds;
initially, she began reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When she reached the end of the scroll—before even a single page was finished—she suddenly suffered from a severe headache.

Upon retiring to bed, it grew even worse. The lady thought to herself, "If I die now, I shall not be able to complete this scripture. Thereupon, she rose and sat up, ordering her maidservant to fetch [water].

She lit a fire, but after a long time she could not get it to burn. As the lady was sighing in lamentation, she suddenly saw a fire enter the hall from the steps and go straight into her bedchamber, hovering about three feet above the ground.
Its brilliance was like that of day. The lady was filled with joy and wonder;

she took up the scripture and recited it, finishing the end of the scroll, whereupon her headache was also cured. After a short while, when the family members arrived with candles, its light immediately vanished. From this time on...
He recited it five times daily as his constant practice. Later, when Lord Rui was about to die, his wife went to visit him.
Lord Rui said to her, "Sister, by the merit of your recitation of the sutras, you shall enjoy long life and be reborn in a good realm.
The lady passed away at the age of eighty. (From *Fayuan zhulin*)

Lady Cui of Boling County was the wife of Wang Chulian of Taiyuan. Chulian’s official career ended with his tenure as the *simā* (vice-president) of Fenzhou, after which the family moved to Hedong in Puzhou.
Their eldest son, Wei, rose to the rank of Right Vice-President of the Department of State Affairs (*shangshu youcheng*).
The second son, Jin, served as Chancellor during the reign of Emperor Daizong. Initially, there was a monk from Hedong named Puji who transmitted the teachings of Shenxiu; once Shenxiu had...

He passed away. An imperial edict appointed Pujì to lead his assembly. During the Kaiyuan era, he resided in the capital by imperial decree. He was grave and dignified, spoke little, and his pure conduct was as pristine as snow.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dàzhào. Cui Shì followed him to study the Buddha-dharma, practicing with diligent devotion.
Wéi built a hall at Wǎnggǔ in Lántiān County to honor his mother; after she had passed away, Wéi submitted a memorial requesting that the estate be donated to establish a monastery. It says:
My late mother, Lady Cui of Boling County, served as a disciple of Great Illumination Chan Master for over thirty years.

Wearing coarse garments and subsisting on simple vegetarian food, she maintained the precepts and dwelt peacefully in meditation, delighting in mountain forests and seeking the tranquility of stillness.
I have therefore established a mountain retreat at Lantian County, where the thatched hall and vihāra, the bamboo groves and fruit orchards, are all places where my deceased parent sat in dhyāna.

...the remainder. At the place where he walked in meditation, when Your Servant encountered a calamity and misfortune, I immediately resolved my mind, vowing to establish a *saṃghārāma* to pursue merit for all eternity.

Furthermore, it coincides with the restoration of the Supreme Sage, whereby all living beings receive blessings. Your Servant, being utterly mediocre and decrepit, has been permitted to participate in this universal journey;

having no means to repay such grace, how could I possibly offer a gift in return? I pray that [Your Majesty] may enjoy a lifespan as vast as heaven, forever serving as the sovereign of the entire realm.

Your Majesty, it is only by relying on the power of the Buddha that my resolve to establish a temple has become so fervent. I venture, out of personal devotion, to intrude upon Your Majesty’s august hearing.
I humbly entreat you to grant this estate as a small monastery and further to appoint seven monks of high virtue from various temples to reside there.

He applied himself with diligence to meditation and recitation, observing the fasts and precepts to uphold the Dharma. He did so to repay the sacred grace of his ancestors above and to requite the loving kindness of his parents below.

His sincerity was beyond measure. An imperial edict granted his request; the temple was named Qingyuan (Clear Source), and the tomb of the Cui family lay to its west. (From the Tang Shu, the collected works of Wang Youcheng, and the Gazetteer of Shaanxi.)
The mother of the beacon-tower guard was a native of Fengzhou. During the Yongtai era, the guard fell into the hands of the Western Tubo.

His mother recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day and prayed before the Buddha, vowing that her son would return alive. The guard came to serve as a standard-bearer for a son of the Btsan-po.
One day, he was granted curd and meat, but he wept bitterly and would not eat them. When asked the reason, he said: "At home, there is an elderly mother who, at night..."

He frequently dreamed that he could not return for a visit, and for this reason he was sorrowful. The Prince of the *btsan-po* took pity on him and spoke to him in private, saying, "The laws of the Tibetan people are strict;
there is no precedent for granting leave to return home. I shall give you two horses; it would be well if you were to escape by way of a secret path.
The watchman took the horses and galloped away, but when the horses' strength was exhausted, they died. He was thus forced to travel on foot, fleeing through the sandy deserts at night.
He was wounded in the foot, and the pain was extreme. Suddenly, the wind blew a scroll of paper past him; he took it and wrapped it around his foot, and the agony of the wound was instantly relieved.
One day, when his mother went to fetch the scriptures, she suddenly tore off several folios. When her son returned home, he removed the paper that had been wrapped around his wound.
Upon examining it, they found that the sutra had been torn away; everyone was greatly astonished and marveled at it as something divine. Yang, the wife of Song Kan, was a native of Jianghuai.
Kan served as a clerk in the Salt and Iron Court. A supervisor of the grain transport convoy invited him to travel north with him.

His wife tried to dissuade him, but he would not listen. Suddenly they encountered a violent storm, and the boat capsized completely. Yuankan entered the water and found a bundle of straw; riding upon it, he reached the shore.
Embracing his bag, he thanked it, saying, "My remaining life is what you have granted me. He carried it back home. After traveling several li, he stayed overnight at an inn.
At dawn, he untied the straw and spread it out to dry; inside was a bamboo tube. Upon opening it, he found gold.
The *Diamond Sūtra* was there. An old woman said to him, "This is the sūtra your wife recites. He returned home, packed his belongings, and told his wife what had happened.
She replied, "It is true. Since you left, I have had someone copy this sūtra for me;
I have been reciting it with great diligence. It has been missing for ten days now. There were some errors in the characters, so I asked another monk to correct them."

It could still be verified. When [Emperor] Qi opened and examined the scripture, it was indeed as such. He sent someone back to the riverbank to search for the shop and the old woman, but neither existed at all.
Several years later, Zheng Yin, the Chancellor, served as the Imperial Commissioner of the Eastern Capital (Dongdu).

He summoned Yankan and his wife, inquired about the full account, and subsequently requested the scripture, which he enshrined within the government offices. He granted official rank to Yankan’s son and provided him with a monthly stipend of cash.
Five thousand [copies]. During the Zhenyuan era, there was also a woman named Wang Conggui, a native of Gong’an.

She regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and had not yet married. Suddenly, she died a violent death. Three days later, when her family went to visit her grave, they heard the sound of moaning.

Upon opening the tomb to look inside, her face appeared as if alive and there was a faint breath from her nostrils. They then carried her back home; after several days, she was able to speak, saying that the officials of the underworld had taken her...

Because she possessed the merit of upholding the sutras, she was released and returned home. Such is the way one attains the noble human path through such causes and conditions (*Youyang Zazhu*, "Records of Retribution").
Pang Xingpo was the wife of the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Xiangyun of Xiangyang.

After the lay practitioner had personally studied under Shitou and attained a profound realization of the ancestral Way, he returned home and preached the Dharma for his wife and children. Both the lady and her daughter, Lingzhao, attained sudden enlightenment at once.
His spiritual acumen was swift and sharp. One day, while a laywoman was hosting a vegetarian feast at Rumon Temple, the *karmadāna* requested her instructions on the occasion.
The laywoman took a comb, tucked it behind her hair, and said, "The dedication of merit has been performed," before departing. Later, Danxia came to visit this laywoman.
Seeing Lingzhao washing vegetables, Danxia asked, "Is the Layman here? Lingzhao set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands folded.
Danxia asked again; Lingzhao took up her basket and walked away. Upon returning, she presented herself to the Layman.

The Layman said, "It is like smearing red earth on top of vermilion. Later, the Layman and Lingzhao were selling a woven bamboo sieve together; as they crossed a bridge, the Layman fell into the water.

As Layman [Dongshan] fell to the ground, Lingzhao also collapsed along with him. The Layman asked, "What is this? Lingzhao replied, "Seeing my father fall to the ground, I have come specifically to support him.
When the Layman was about to enter nirvana, he said to Lingzhao, "Go out and see what time it is, and report back when it is noon.
Lingzhao went out the door and quickly reported, "The sun has already reached its zenith, yet there is an eclipse. The Layman rose from his seat and approached the window.
Lingzhao then sat cross-legged upon her mat and passed away. The layman gathered firewood and cremated her; shortly thereafter, he also passed away.
Someone ran to inform the grandmother, who said, "This foolish daughter and this ignorant old man have departed without notifying one another;

how can they bear to do this? She then went to tell her son. Her son was just then clearing a field for cultivation; laying down his hoe, he responded, "Aha! and looking at them, he immediately passed away.
After the cremation was completed, the old woman traveled through the villages and neighborhoods to bid farewell; it was not known where she ended her days (*Chuan Deng Lu*, *Record of Layman Pang*).
As for the "Old Woman Who Brewed Tea," no one knew her origins. Magu and Nanquan, accompanied by a monk, were heading toward Mount Jing when they encountered the old woman on the road.
She asked them, "Which way does the path to Mount Jing go? The old woman replied, "Go straight ahead. Magu...
He asked, "The water ahead is deep; can you cross it? The old woman said, "My feet will not get wet.
He spoke again, "The rice on the upper bank is so lush, while the rice on the lower bank is so frail. The old woman said, "It has all been eaten by the crabs. He spoke yet again.
The grain was fragrant. The old woman said, "It has no breath. She asked where the old woman lived, and she replied, "I live right here.
When the three men reached the shop, the old woman brewed a pot of tea and brought out three cups, saying, "If you monks possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), then drink this tea.
While the three looked at one another, the old woman said, "Watch as I myself display my supernatural powers," and immediately—
He lifted his cup, poured out some tea, and departed (*Chuan Deng Lu*).
As for Zheng Shisan Niang, her place of residence is unknown. At the age of twelve, she followed an *shiguo* (nun-teacher) to visit Chan Master Da Mui.
The Master asked, "Where does this nun reside? The nun replied, "I live by the banks of the Nantai River. The Master shouted.
He came out. The Master asked, "Where does Zheng reside? Zheng stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. The Master asked again.
Zheng said, "I have already presented myself to the Master. The Master said, "Go.

When Zheng reached the Dharma Hall, the nun said, "Thirteen's Daughter usually says she understands Chan, but today, when questioned by the Great Master, she was completely speechless. Zheng said, "What a pity!"

"How bitter! To have such eyes as these, yet still claim to be traveling on pilgrimage. [He] took off his patched robe and gave it to Shisan Niang. The sister-in-law of Master Píngtián Ān was the wife of Master Píngtián Ān. When Línjì visited Ān, he encountered his sister-in-law in the field driving the oxen.

He already possesses the intent to pull out nails and extract wedges. When he met Da'an, Da'an asked, "Have you seen my sister-in-law yet?

The old woman who sold cakes was a person of unknown origin. When Chan Master Deshan Jian first lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he composed the *Qinglong Shuchao* (Blue Dragon Commentary).
Hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, he felt deeply unsettled and intended to go there to convert and guide them.
He then carried his notes on the *Qinglong* [Commentary] out of Shu. On his way, he passed through Liyang and encountered an old woman selling cakes.
He bought a cake for a snack. The woman asked what book he was carrying; he replied, "The *Qinglong* Notes. She asked which sutra he lectured upon; he said, "The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The woman said, "I have a question. If you can answer it, I will give you this snack; if you cannot answer it, you had better go elsewhere. She then quoted from the sutra:
He said, "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.

I do not know which mind the Elder is pointing to. The Master remained silent. He then went to Longtan to study under Chan Master Xin, where he attained sudden enlightenment regarding the essential point of the mind.
He took his commentaries and notes and burned them (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
Ling Xingpo’s native place was unknown. She once visited Chan Master Fubei and asked, "To whom should one entrust that phrase which cannot be attained even by exerting one's full strength?
The Master said, "Fubei has no superfluous words. Ling Xingpo said, "I have not yet reached Fubei."
"Do not hesitate to harbor doubt," the Master said. "If you have another depth of realization, do not hesitate to bring it forth. The old woman folded her hands and wept, saying, "Alas!
To my bitter suffering, heaven adds yet more grievance. The Master was speechless. The woman said, "In words, you do not know the biased from the correct;
in principle, you do not recognize the inverted from the upright. To act as a teacher for others is to invite calamity. Later, a monk reported this to Nanquan. Nanquan said, "What a pity for Fubei!"
Having been thus rebuked by the old woman, the monk Chengyi passed her by. The old woman laughed and said, "Master Wang still lacks a bit of expedient means.
Chengyi asked, "What is it that Master Nanquan still lacks? The old woman then wept, saying, "How tragic!
How painful! Chengyi was at a loss for what to do. The old woman asked, "Do you understand? Chengyi stood there with palms joined. The old woman—
He said, "There are as many dead Zen practitioners as there are sesame seeds and millet grains. Chengyi once brought up the case of Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, 'If I had seen this old woman, I would have questioned her until her mouth was mute. Chengyi asked, 'I wonder, Master, how would you have questioned her?
Zhaozhou then struck him. Chengyi said, 'Why did you strike me instead? Zhaozhou replied, 'Because you are like a dead man.'"
"If you do not strike me, what are you waiting for? He struck her several times in succession. The old woman heard this and laughed, saying, "Zhaozhou deserves to receive my staff.
Someone reported this to Zhaozhou, who wept and said, "How tragic! How painful!
When the old woman heard of this, she joined her palms and sighed, "Zhaozhou’s eye pierces through the four worlds. Zhaozhou then sent a monk to ask her, "What is the Eye of Zhaozhou? The old woman—
He then raised his fist. The monk returned and told Zhaozhou about it. Zhaozhou composed a verse, saying: "When the occasion arises, he presents it face-to-face;

The Master’s wailing cry has already ceased; now that dawn has broken, who knows it? At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha, how many lost the opportunity before their eyes?
(From the *Chuan Deng Lu*). As for Li Xingpo, her place of residence is unknown. She once attended upon Chan Master Kuang of Tanzhou. The Master asked, "Do you remember?"
"Are you from the time [you were] at Jiangzhou? The old woman said, "It would not be known without you, Master.
The Master said, "Much empty talk and little substance. The old woman said, "What is there to hide? The Master said, "I am mindful that you are a woman; I let you go with your staff.
The old woman said, "I, this humble one, never see any fault in a venerable elder. The Master said, "Where does the old monk’s fault lie? The old woman said, "The Master has no fault."
The old woman said, "How could I have committed an offense? The Master asked, "What about one who has committed no offense?
The old woman then held up her fist and said, "In this way, everything becomes topsy-turvy. The Master said, "Truly, there is nowhere to hide" (*Chuan Deng Lu*).

The Old Woman of Mount Wutai was a person of unknown origin. A monk traveling to the Five Terraces encountered her on the road and asked, "In which direction does the path to the Terrace Mountains go?
The old woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed. The old woman remarked, "What a fine monk, yet he goes off in such a manner.
Later, another monk related this incident to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Wait until I go to investigate him myself."
The next day, Zhaozhou set out. He asked the old woman, "Which way does the road to Mount Tai go? The woman said, "Go straight ahead. Zhaozhou went straight on.
The woman said, "What a fine monk, yet he goes off like that! Zhaozhou returned to the monastery and said to the monks:
"The old woman of Mount Tai has been thoroughly exposed by you. Furthermore, there was another old woman who sent someone with money to Zhaozhou, requesting that he recite the Tripitaka.
Zhaozhou accepted the offering, then descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "Tell the old woman that the recitation of the Tripitaka is finished.
When the messenger returned and reported this to the old woman, she asked, "I have always requested the complete Tripitaka; why did he say it was finished?"
He merely recited half of the *Āgama* collection. Furthermore, an old woman encountered Zhaozhou on the road. Zhaozhou asked, "Where are you going?
She replied, "I am going to steal Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots. Zhaozhou said, "What will you do when you encounter me? The old woman then gave him a slap, and Zhaozhou ceased his questioning.
On another occasion, an old woman entered Zhaozhou’s Dharma Hall while the meal was being served. The old woman said, "The monks in this hall—"
It is always what is born of the grandmother. Only this eldest child was disobedient and unfilial. As soon as Zhaozhou looked back, the old woman departed.
While Zhaozhou was walking through the fields, he encountered an old woman planting them. Zhaozhou asked, "What would you do if you suddenly encountered a fierce tiger?
The old woman said, "There is not a single dharma that can be taken as an object of the mind. Zhaozhou said, "Ha! The old woman also said, "Ha! Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "There is still this one remaining. Another old woman entered the monastery late in the evening. Zhaozhou asked, "What is it?
The woman replied, "I am here to stay the night. Zhaozhou said, "What place is this? The woman laughed loudly and departed (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
He Chen’s wife, Lady Liu, was a native of Jingzhou. From her youth, she abstained from alcohol and meat and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

She made a vow before the Buddha, pledging that her life would end at the age of forty-five. She knew the day of her death in advance; in the fourth year of the Taihe era, she reached the age of forty-five.

She gave away all her belongings to provide for the Sangha and took leave of all her relatives and friends. On the eve of the New Year, she invited monks to receive the eightfold precepts of the fast.
She bathed, changed her clothes, and sat cross-legged in a single room, chanting the sutras aloud. Afterward, she became silent.

When dawn broke, her children pushed open the door and entered, only to find she had passed away; the heat of her crown was such that it could burn the hand. Zhěn buried her according to the rites for a monk in the north.
In the *Youyang zazu*, it is recorded that Yao Po was a native of Shangdang who was close friends with Fan Po.
Fan Po exhorted her to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, and Yao Po followed her advice.
She subsequently set aside all domestic affairs and focused her mind single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name. At the time of her death, she beheld Amitābha Buddha descending before her.
In mid-air, two bodhisattvas stood in attendance at his left and right. Yao Po addressed the Buddha, saying, "If I had not met Fan Po, how could I have seen the Buddha?
I beg you, World-Honored One, to stay for a short while so that I may bid her farewell. When Fan Po arrived, the Buddha remained as solemn and majestic as before;
Yao Po then immediately ascended into transformation (to the Pure Land).
Wen Jingwen’s wife was from Bingzhou. She had been bedridden for a long time due to illness. Jingwen instructed her to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, and she followed his advice.
She silently chanted the Buddha’s name without ceasing for two years. One day, she told Jingwen, "I have already seen the Buddha."
She was certain to pass away the following month. Three days before her death, a lotus flower appeared before her, as large as the sun's disk.

When the appointed time arrived, she prepared food and offered it to her parents, saying: "I am now fortunate to have been born in the Pure Land. I pray that my parents and husband will single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha;
then we shall meet. Having spoken these words, she passed away. (From the *Jingtu wen*)
The woman who burned the hermitage was a person of unknown origin. She had served a single hermit master for nearly twenty years, constantly sending a young girl to deliver his meals.
One day, she directed the girl to step forward and press close to him, saying, "At this very moment, what is it like?
The monk replied, "A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; throughout the three winters, there is no warmth. The girl reported this to the woman, and the woman said, "I..."
For twenty years, she had served nothing but an ordinary layman, so she finally sent a monk out to burn down her hut (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
Laywoman Chen Dao was from Wenzhou; she once visited various renowned masters before attaining enlightenment through the words of Master Shan Jing.
She composed a verse which says: "On the level summit of the high hill, There are only woodcutters; Every person carries a blade within their breast."
The Intent of the Axe. One does not see mountain flowers reflecting red in the water (from the *Chuanteng lu*).

Lady Zhongli Ren was the mother of Zhongli Jin of Kuaiji, who served as the Governor of Kaifeng during the Song dynasty. Throughout her life, she was deeply devoted to the practice of pure karma (*śuddha-karma*).
She carved sandalwood (*candana*) into an image of Amitābha Buddha and would constantly wear it upon her head while practicing the Way. At the age of ninety...

Fen also devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. At the time of his death, he said of himself: "My lady has informed me that the time for my rebirth has arrived.

Lady Wang of Yueguo was the wife of Prince Jing, the paternal uncle of Emperor Zhezong. She devoted herself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism without ceasing day or night.
She led her handmaidens and servants to share her resolve for rebirth in the Western Paradise. Among them was one servant who alone grew indolent;

the Lady said, "I cannot allow you, a single person, to ruin my discipline," and she cast her out. The servant was struck with fear and remorse, whereupon she roused her spirit and applied herself with diligence.
She advanced [in her practice], remaining untiring for a long time. One day, she said to her colleagues, "It is time for me to depart.

That night, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, and she passed away without illness. The following night, a colleague informed the lady, saying, "Last night I dreamed of the maidservant who has transformed and departed."

She was instructed to convey her thanks to the Lady, saying: "I am most fortunate to have received your reprimand; I shall be reborn in the Western Paradise, and my gratitude for your virtue is immeasurable.
The Lady said, "If he can enter my dream, then I shall believe you. That evening, the Lady dreamed that the maidservant conveyed her thanks as before.
The Lady asked, "Can one reach the Western Paradise? The maid replied, "Yes," and then led the Lady along. After a short while, they saw a great...
In the pond were lotus flowers of various sizes interspersed, some flourishing and others withered.

The lady asked for the reason, and the maidservant replied, "For those in this world who cultivate the Western Paradise, a single flower arises here for every single thought they generate; thus, the flowers differ according to whether their practice is diligent or lax."
Their flourishing and decline are also different: those who are diligent flourish, while those who are indolent and negligent wither away.

If one perseveres without ceasing over a long period, until mindfulness is matured and contemplation is perfected, then when the body dissolves and the spirit departs, one will certainly be reborn therein. Among them was a person sitting in court robes, adorned with a precious crown and necklaces.
The lady asked, "Who is this? The maid replied, "This is Yang Jie. There was another person as well.
He was sitting in his court robes, his countenance somewhat haggard. The lady asked again, "Who is this? He replied, "It is Ma Xu.

At that time, Zhiqie had already passed away, while Xu remained alive; both had cultivated the Pure Land, yet Zhiqie’s realization and practice were complete, and his perfection in both compassion and wisdom was especially unsurpassed.
The lady asked, "Where shall I be reborn? A maidservant led her along the path.
After traveling several *li*, she saw from afar a flower pedestal, its gold and azure glinting brilliantly, its radiance penetrating and clear.
Her maidservant said, "This is the place where the mistress will be born; it is the highest grade of birth upon the Golden Terrace. Upon waking, sorrow and joy welled up within her simultaneously.
On the morning of her birthday that year, she took up an incense burner, lit the incense, and stood gazing toward the Hall of Avalokiteśvara, while her kinsmen were just then approaching.

He did so for the sake of her longevity; when he looked at her, she had already passed away. During the Xuanhong era, Huang Ce, a Court Official (Zhige), recorded this event as the *Record of the Rebirth of the Lady of Yueguo* (*Yuebang wenlei*).

Lady Chen was a native of Qiantang. She received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Lingzhi and devoted herself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, performing a thousand prostrations daily.
From between her sutra desk and the altar, śarīras (relics) emerged. At the time of her death, she saw the Buddha coming to welcome her;
she looked back and spoke to those beside her, but before she had finished speaking, she passed away peacefully (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Lady Yuan was a native of Qiantang. She received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Lingzhi and immediately abstained from meat and alcohol, devotedly cultivating the Pure Land practice.
Her family members were all transformed by her example. After twenty years had passed in this manner, she manifested illness one day and invited Vinaya Master Yuanjing to preach the Dharma for her.
Suddenly, she beheld a multitude of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appearing before her to welcome and guide her; she then passed away while sitting upright (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Lady Chen was the mother of Chan Master Jielu of Changlu. The Master once compiled the *Record of the Lotus Supreme Assembly* to universally exhort both monastics and laypeople to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise.
While residing at Puhui Monastery in Guangping, he invited his mother to live in the eastern chamber of the abbot’s quarters.
Morning and evening he recited the Buddha’s name. Later, he fell ill; he gathered the assembly and led them in chanting the Buddha’s name for two full days.

Suddenly, with palms joined and gazing at a Buddha image, he passed away peacefully. On the day before his death, the Master had dreamed that his mother said to him, "I see more than ten nuns coming to summon you.
The Master replied, "This is an auspicious sign of rebirth in the Pure Land. Having spoken, he sat upright and died, his face as radiant as white jade. Thus he passed away.
The following day, her crown was slightly warm and her face was bright, just as she had seen in her dream (*Fozu Tongji*).
Lady Yu was the daughter of the Qin family of Qiantang; her husband made his living by selling fish. Having a son who fell into legal trouble, he ruined the family, leaving the lady in deep distress.
Desiring to drown herself in the river, she encountered Master Zhao of Jingzhu Temple, who exhorted her, saying: "In a previous life..."
"Karmic conditions must all be accepted with equanimity. To drown yourself pointlessly in the river is not as good as reciting the Buddha's name.

The old woman was deeply awakened and immediately lit a finger before the Buddha, vowing to observe a perpetual fast and recite the Buddha’s name every day without fail for ten years. She addressed everyone she met as a "Son of the Buddha.
One day, she invited a monk to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, while she herself held a rosary and recited the Buddha’s name.
Name: [Omitted]. According to the *Fozu tongji*, she passed away in tranquility during the chapter on "Contemplating the Buddha’s Image.

A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
all things are created solely by the mind. One night, he dreamed that the Lord of Hell came to thank him, saying:

The nun Kongshimdao was named Zhitong; she was the daughter of Fan Xun, a Grand Marshal of the Dragon Chart (Longtu).
Intelligent and wise from childhood, she grew up to marry Ti, the grandson of Chancellor Su Song. Not long after, she grew weary of worldly entanglements and returned home to seek ordination.

Her father opposed this, so she remained alone to practice ascetic cultivation. Upon reading the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, she attained realization and composed two verses. The first says: "Vast and boundless is the dust of the world..."

At the limit of exhaustion, both movement and stillness are perfectly pervasive and unobstructed. Later, when his parents had both passed away, his elder brother Jian took up the post of Magistrate of Fenning.

Cui Po was a native of Zizhou and had been a wet nurse for the Liang family of Dongping. She was a person of simple and honest character who had abstained from meat and blood since her youth.

Her mistress, Lady Chao, took a keen interest in Chan studies; while attending to her, Cui Po would do nothing but recite the name of Amitābha Buddha every day without interruption, and she never kept track of the number of times she did so.

Tao Shi was a native of Changshu. After the death of his wife, he lived alone and regularly recited the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter).

Lady Li was the wife of Mr. Hu of Shangyu. After her husband’s death, she recited the names of the Buddhas and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* day and night without ceasing, her voice resonating throughout both the interior and exterior of the house for more than ten years.

On the following day, a flower grew at the site of the cremation; it was white in color and more than two inches in circumference, though its name remains unknown (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Sheng’ao was a native of Qiantang. Daily she recited the names of the Buddhas and concurrently studied the *Sūtra on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*.
Before long, she fell ill. One morning she rose, instructed her attendants to prepare a bath, and once finished, sat upright facing west.

She asked those around her, "Do you hear the sound of the chime? The holy assembly of the Pure Land is about to arrive. Shortly thereafter, she joined her palms, smiled, and said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already [arrived]."
When she arrived, a golden platform appeared before her. "I shall now depart," she said, and having finished speaking, she passed away (*Fozu Tongji*). Lady Huang was a native of Mingzhou.

A single lotus flower sprouted [from her grave] (*Fozu tongji*).

A daughter of the Wang family from Jixian, she had admired the practice of Pure Land Buddhism since her youth. Daily, she recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, the *Avalokiteśvara*, and the *Vajracchedikā* sūtras.

Her mother fell ill and passed away. As they were about to prepare her for burial, blood flowed from her body and soaked it. The daughter vowed, saying, "If my filial piety is sincere and true, may no foul odor arise from my mother's body.

Zhoupo was a native of Taiping. She had cultivated the practice of purity from her youth, and as she grew old, she became increasingly devout.

The daughter of the Pei family was a native of Fenyang. She lived in purity and dedicated herself exclusively to the practice of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha).

Since you have now released the grievance, your life shall also be extended. From this time forth, Emperor Yuanzong recited the mantra with increasing devotion;

The woman of the Chen family was named Miaozhen. She was a native of Lishui, Chuzhou. Her father served as the ritual attendant at a shrine and died young;
her mother remarried into another clan. Miaozhen lived with her grandmother, Lin. When Lin fell ill, Miaozhen cut flesh from her own thigh [to prepare medicine].
He mixed it with spoiled venison and served it to him. When the illness had slightly abated, someone informed Lin; Lin wept bitterly in self-reproach, and the illness returned as before.
Miaozhen then sold her clothes and ran to a Buddhist temple to perform various rites for averting calamity, but to no avail.

She then burned incense upon her right arm and, prostrating herself with her forehead to the ground, cried out to Heaven, praying that she might take his place. On the night of the *renshen* day in the fourth month of the fourth year of Zhizheng...
She dreamed of a man wearing a black silk cap and a blue cloth robe who came to tell her, "Do not worry;
if you can cut out your liver to feed your grandmother, she will recover. When she asked where she should go to cut it, the man pointed to her right flank.
He then had her swallow half a pill of red medicine; having swallowed it, she immediately awoke. On the day of Jiashu, Miaozhen again prepared herself with a bath and cleansing.
They bathed and offered prayers outdoors to the deities above and below. At that time, it rained; yet when it reached Miaozhen’s body, she alone remained unsullied by moisture.

She leaned down to pick it up, and her liver suddenly protruded, hanging downward. She quickly cut it off and placed it upon a table, vowing:

She sliced the liver, mixed it with bamboo shoots, and cooked it to serve to Lin. Lin ate it and found it delicious; his illness was immediately cured, while Miaozhen’s wound was so severe that she nearly perished. Then [the liver] returned.
A dream deity spoke to her, saying, "There is no harm. Simply prepare paper into ash and apply it to the wound. Following these words, the wound healed as it was before.
At that time, Miaozhen was fourteen years old. Three years later, Lin passed away from natural causes.
